meta.title: Retaining Walls in Rochester Hills, MI | HD Landscape
meta.description: Low block retaining walls and raised bed borders for sloped Rochester Hills, MI yards, with the city's steep slope rules talked through. Free estimates.

hero.kicker: Retaining walls in Rochester Hills, MI
hero.title: That bank is a level bed **waiting for a wall.**
hero.lede: A low block wall from HD Landscape turns a Rochester Hills slope into a level bed or more usable lawn. A good one rises from a firm base with drainage behind the block, and the city's slope rules come before the first shovel.

local.title: A low wall helps here, if the slope allows it.
local.intro: City code sorts steep ground by how sharp it is and how far it drops, from moderate slopes at 20 percent up to bluffs at 40 percent and more. Plenty of banks fall outside all of that. The first job is working out which kind you have, because some come with rules.

points.title: Low walls that make flat ground
points.body: A short wall at the bottom of a bank can give you a level bed or a wider lawn above it. Low block walls are what we build. Walls over about 4 feet, or walls holding up a driveway, usually need an engineer first.

points.title: Regulated steep slopes
points.body: City code covers slopes of 25 percent and steeper with 10 feet or more of drop, and slopes from 20 percent within 200 feet of the Clinton River, Paint Creek, Sargent Creek, Stony Creek and their tributaries. New walls or grading there can take a Steep Slope Permit, so confirm yours with the city.

points.title: Room at the top
points.body: The code also measures a setback from the top of a regulated slope: 15, 25 or 50 feet, by slope class. So a wall planned near the crest can be caught by the rule even if it looks like it sits on the flat part. Ask the city about the top of the bank as well as the bottom.

points.title: One foot up, three feet over
points.body: The city's guidebook for accessory structures caps graded slopes at 1 foot of rise for every 3 feet of run, and says steeper grades call for retaining walls with construction details. It is written for sheds and garages, but a bank steeper than that may need a wall for more than looks.

points.title: Pipes the city does not own
points.body: A sump line belongs to the owner of the lot, and many other shared pipes belong to the development or association. Buried lines get marked before digging, but private ones are easy to miss, so tell us about anything you know is down there.

logistics.title: A wall starts with the base you never see.
body: The first look is at the slope itself: how high it is, what it holds and which way the rain runs. If the wall would sit near a creek or on a steep bank, Jake will point you to the city before anything gets dug.

A wall that lasts goes up in order: a trench, a firm packed base, a level first row, then block rising with gravel behind it and soil packed in along the way. Most of what decides how long it stays straight ends up buried.

faq.q: Do you build retaining walls in Rochester Hills?
faq.a: Yes. HD Landscape builds low block retaining walls and raised bed borders in Rochester Hills. Walls over about 4 feet usually need an engineer, and if a slope needs more than a low wall, [yard grading](/yard-grading/) or a series of shorter walls may be the better answer.

faq.q: Does a retaining wall need a permit in Rochester Hills?
faq.a: That turns on the height, what the wall holds up and where it sits. New work on a regulated steep slope can take a Steep Slope Permit, and taller walls or walls carrying extra load are where permits and engineering usually come in. Rules change, so call the city's Building Department before the first block goes in.

faq.q: Does fixing an old retaining wall on a slope take a permit in Rochester Hills?
faq.a: A repair usually does not need a Steep Slope Permit. The city's steep slope rules allow maintenance and repair of existing retaining walls without one, while a new wall is treated differently. If a wall has failed and needs rebuilding, ask the city which side of that line it falls on. Jake can look at it and give you his advice.

faq.q: How do I know if my slope is regulated in Rochester Hills?
faq.a: It comes down to steepness, height and where the slope sits. Very steep slopes and bluffs are regulated anywhere in the city, and moderate ones only within 200 feet of the named creeks and their tributaries. Moderate and very steep slopes of 5,000 square feet or less are exempt, and man made slopes can sometimes be waived. The city makes the final call.

faq.q: Can a retaining wall go near a creek in Rochester Hills?
faq.a: Sometimes, but expect a conversation with the city first. City code generally keeps a 25 foot setback from natural features, where filling, grading and moving materials are barred unless the city reduces it. Plans approved before January 17, 1990 may be treated differently.
